component.name: rhYciv
component.summary: A crisp, high-resolution turn-based empire strategy game

description.p: rhYciv is a classic turn-based empire strategy game with a modern high-resolution renderer, deeper zoom, streamlined conquest rules, and attributed open-source artwork.
The bundled rules, interface data, fonts, and art make this a standalone game; no commercial game installation is required.
The interface, from a full pass over the 0.1.5 report.

Every message the game shows is narrower and taller — they were set to nearly two thirds of the screen, about a hundred and forty characters to a line, and are now set to roughly the measure of a book. Messages also wait their turn: one comes up at a time, nothing arrives over the top of a battle still being played out, and zooming to a city on a disorder report no longer gets the next report dropped on top of the city window.

The Go To dialog can be left again — Cancel was being read as the show-all-cities toggle and reopened the dialog instead of closing it. Find City now takes the map to the city; its Ok did nothing at all. Typing a letter at any list jumps to the next entry under it, and city names in lists are bigger.

Squares on a city's resource map can all be clicked: the click worked out which square you meant with completely different arithmetic from the one that drew it, and squares they disagreed about could not be selected. Taking a city names it and opens it, losing one says so, a city's size beside its name keeps up with what it builds, and a sleeping unit wakes when something hostile steps alongside. An expensive item's production shields fill the box in rows rather than collapsing to a single line.
Combat draws from the game's own seeded generator now, so a battle can be replayed from a saved game's seed. A starving city disbands a settler it supports before it loses a citizen, as Civ II does.

You can change how you are governed. REVOLUTION has been in the Kingdom menu since the menus were written with nothing behind it, so a civilisation was handed Despotism at the start and stayed under it for the whole game however far it researched. A revolution now costs two turns of anarchy, after which your people ask what they are to become, and researching a government offers the revolution there and then.

Diplomats and Spies do something at last. Everything the Diplomat asks to show — the offer to bribe a unit, the price of inciting a city — was missing from the game's text, so nothing was ever shown and the unit stood there having achieved nothing. Investigate City and Steal Technology are new: an agent brings back an account of a rival city, garrison included, or carries out one of its owner's secrets. A city can only be robbed once. A Diplomat does not come home from any of it; a Spy does, having spent a move.
The game answers the keyboard and the mouse again.

One press of End Turn now plays a whole turn. Starting a civilisation's turn handed control back and waited, which is right for you and wrong for everybody else — a computer civilisation has nothing that comes back later to ask it to carry on, so each rival moved a single unit and then held the turn. With eight rivals on the board that meant pressing Enter eight times, into a game that appeared to be ignoring you, before you could move again. Rival civilisations also move their whole armies now, and their fortify and settler orders actually resolve.

Keypresses are no longer lost. Keys were read by asking about every key on the keyboard once a frame, so a key pressed and released during a frame that ran long had already come back up before it was asked about, and the press simply never happened. Redrawing the map is about ten times faster, a redraw happens when it is asked for instead of waiting up to two seconds on the animation clock, and the side panel keeps answering the mouse after it rebuilds itself.

The research chooser has a Goal button: name an advance to work towards and it lists only the research that leads there, or says plainly when nothing you can begin now brings it any nearer. The goal is remembered in saved games and retires itself when it is reached.
Saving, and a turn that ends when you press Enter.

Save Game and Load Game are in the Game menu and work when clicked; before this they were drawn but carried no action, and saving was only reachable by a keyboard shortcut. "Autosave each turn" has been a checkbox for a long time and now actually writes, three rotating slots taken at the start of each turn. Opening the Save dialog could take the game down before it drew, if the leader's name was shorter than two characters.

Ending a turn no longer takes several presses of Enter. It stopped at the first unit that needed a decision and abandoned the rest of the army, so the units behind it were never processed at all -- a unit told to fortify did not become fortified until whatever preceded it had been dealt with.
Diplomats can buy units and cities. A lone unit in the open can be bribed, a garrison comes with the city it defends, and a capital cannot be bought at any price.

Huts use the original game's measured odds: five outcomes at one chance in five each, with no empty village among them. The coastline is dark water meeting a thread of beach instead of a lit turquoise outline, the generation matte is gone from the citizens and the city roofs, production shields are drawn as an even block, and the marker for a unit killed in combat appears -- it never once did.
The map, from a full beta test.

Roads and railways now meet at the edges of a square instead of scattering as dashes across it, and rivers run as rivers: the sixteen river tiles are drawn to match which neighbours the water actually reaches, and a river arriving at the coast opens into a mouth instead of stopping. An ocean square is drawn as water whatever surrounds it, so a one-square bay is no longer a meadow with whales breaching out of it. Irrigation and farmland are ploughed fields rather than a blue lattice, and the goody hut, the flag over a city and the resource icons are all drawn from the high-resolution art set.

A road is worth a third of a movement point to every unit again, not only to those with more than one point to spend — settlers, warriors and musketeers were walking their own roads at one square a turn. Pressing Enter ends a turn, and the side panel says when the game is waiting for it. When a unit is killed the map holds on the square long enough to see it happen, and marks it. Huts hold something worth finding far more often than they hold nothing, a new city starts building something it can actually build, and the map no longer scrolls off to watch movement the player is not entitled to see.
Fixes a crash introduced in 0.1.1.

Founding a city could leave the game with no unit to move, and asking for the next one then recursed until the process died. It left no crash report, because the failure was a stack overflow, which cannot be caught. Anyone on 0.1.1 should update.
Fixes two crashes and a round of interface problems reported against 0.1.0.

Saving failed permanently once the barbarians had taken a city, and researching an advance that enabled a terrain improvement took the game down. Units and improvements in the Change Production list are drawn at a readable size instead of a few pixels, and the list keeps a stable order so something unlocked by a new advance appears where you would look for it rather than at the bottom. A unit that has finished its turn stops blinking, a unit that slept to heal wakes when it is whole, and disbanding a unit clears it from the city window at once. The city window is finished in the same painted stone as the rest of the interface.
The first release built for Linux, Windows and macOS together, and the first that is not a beta.

Roads and railways are painted art rather than drawn lines, and connect correctly to each of a tile's eight neighbours. The city window is finished in the same stone as the rest of the interface instead of flat grey. The project has been separated from its upstream fork: the solution, the projects, the engine namespace and the save directory all carry the rhYciv name, and saves written by earlier builds are migrated on first launch. Every change is now checked by continuous integration on all three platforms.
